items: Given a list of names, decide whether any name appears twice . "Alice" appears twice, so the answer is "yes". Solution one: compare everything with everything. Take the first name and check it against everyone after it, then the second, and so on. Solution two: remember as you go. Keep a set of names already seen, and check each new one against it. Both give the right answer. And that's exactly where the real question begins. Build lists that contain no duplicates at all (so both functions must run to completion before answering "no"), then time them: Measured on an ordinary laptop (Python 3.10): At n=8000 the nested loop takes nearly a second; the set takes 0.0002 seconds — 4000× apart. It comes down to how many comparisons happen . Solution one (nested loops): with n items, the first is compared n-1 times, the second n-2 times… totalling roughly n = 100 → about 5 000 n = 1000 → about 500 000 n = 8000 → about 32 million Solution two (set): each item is looked up exactly once, so exactly n lookups. n = 100 → 100 n = 1000 → 1000 n = 8000 → 8000 Spot the pattern. When n doubles: solution one does 4× the comparisons (it's n²) solution two does 2× the comparisons (it's n) The measureme

You might think timing is enough. It isn't , because the same program takes wildly different times depending on context: Factor Effect --- --- Machine speed the same code can be 5× slower on older hardware Language a nested loop in C may beat a single loop in Python The data itself a duplicate early on means an early return, so it finishes fast Current load a background download makes everything slower So we need a measure that's independent of the machine and describes the algorithm itself. That's big-O. O(f(n)) means: as the input size n grows large, the number of operations doesn't grow faster than f(n). Three points: 1. Only the growth trend matters, not the exact number. 3n operations → O(n) 3n + 100 operations → still O(n) n²/2 + 5n operations → O(n²) 2. Constant factors are dropped. O(2n) and O(n) are the same thing, because the trend is identical: double n, double the time. 3. Only the highest-order term survives. O(n² + n) becomes O(n²), because for large n the n² term swamps the n term entirely: 2n in total → O(n) (drop the constant 2) n × n = n² → O(n²) Whether n is 10 or 10 million, these lines do a fixed amount of work → O(1) Note: O(1) doesn't mean "one operation" — i

You have a sorted array. Find two numbers that add up to a target, and return their indices. This works. It is also O(n²): for n = 6 it checks 15 pairs, for n = 1000 it checks about 500,000. Here is the thing nobody tells you: almost all of those checks are pointless. Look at what happens when i = 0 (value 1): With target = 12, as soon as 1 + 11 = 12 we are done. But suppose target = 18: Once 1 + 11 < 18, we know for free that 1 + 3, 1 + 5, 1 + 7, 1 + 9 are all too small too. The inner loop did five checks to learn one fact. That is the waste. The array is sorted, so the largest possible partner tells you everything. Put left at the start and right at the end: Run it and you see the whole journey: Four steps instead of fifteen. And each step is forced — there is no other move that could possibly work. The whole trick rests on one sentence: So at each step there is exactly one thing to do: Situation What you know Move --- --- --- sum == target done stop sum < target even the biggest partner is not enough → this left is hopeless left += 1 sum > target even the smallest partner is too much → this right is hopeless right -= 1 "Hopeless" is the key word. A lot of problems ask you to modify an array in place (no new array allowed) and return the length of the "valid" portion. Typical scenarios: Deduplicate a sorted array (keep exactly one copy of each value) Remove every element equal to a given value Move all zeros to the end If you were allowed to build a new list, all of these would be trivial. But when the constraint says O(1) extra space , you need slow/fast pointers. Slow pointer slow : points at "the next free slot where an answer element can be written" Fast pointer fast : walks all the way through, hunting for "useful elements" Every time fast finds a useful element, copy it into slow's slot, then advance slow by one. Problem : given nums and val, remove all elements equal to val in place and return the new length. Approach : fast visits every element; slow marks the next writable slot. Anything that is not val gets to stay. Trace nums = [3, 2, 2, 3, 4], val = 3: Time O(n), space O(1) — only two pointer variables are used. Problem : given an array of positive integers and a target value, find the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is >= target , and return its length. Brute force : enumerate every start, then enumerate every end. Time O(n²) . At n = 100,000 this times out. The problem with brute force is: every time the start moves one step right, you sum from scratch . But the new interval and the old one overlap heavily, so you can reuse that work. Sliding window approach : left: left boundary of the window right: right boundary (keeps expanding) window sum: sum of the elements currently inside the window Two operations : 1. Expand : move right right, add nums[right] into the window sum 2. Shrink : once the window sum >= target, record the length, then move left right, subtracting nums[left] from the window sum Key point : both left and right only ever move forward — neither ever steps backward. right goes from 0 to n-1: at most n steps left goes from 0 to n-1: at most n steps The two pointers take at most 2n steps combined -> O(n). Compared with brute force's O(n²), this is a qualitative leap. nums = [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3], target = 7: How the window changes : Every shrink asks the same question:

Given an integer array nums, find every triple [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i < j < k and the three values add up to 0. The answer must not contain duplicate triples. Why sort at all? Because a sorted array unlocks two-pointer techniques , and sorting also herds equal values together, which makes dedup possible. Sorting costs O(n log n) — far less than the brute-force O(n³) we are about to get rid of. Brute force uses three nested loops, O(n³). The optimization rests on one idea: Finding two numbers — that is exactly the two-sum problem from lesson 06. But now the array is sorted, so you can solve it in O(n) with collision pointers . Outer loop O(n), inner two-pointer O(n) → overall O(n²). This is the tricky part. The problem demands no duplicate triples . If nums[i] == nums[i-1], the current element is the same as the previous one. So the triples you find by pinning it will be identical to the ones you already found in the last round → skip it. Once you find a valid triple, left and right may still be pointing at copies of the same element. You must skip them. nums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4] → after sorting [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2] Step Complexity --- --- sort O(n log n) outer

Problem : You are given an array and repeatedly asked "what is the sum of elements in the interval [l, r]?" The naive approach: for every query, accumulate from scratch. Every query costs O(n). If you ask 100,000 times, the total work is 100,000 × n — a guaranteed timeout. If you spend O(n) up front to compute and store all the "prefix" information, then every subsequent query becomes O(1). This is the idea of prefix sums . Definition : prefix[i] stores the sum of all elements in nums[0..i-1] (the sum of the first i elements). How to compute prefix : O(n) once, use forever. Sum of interval [l, r] = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] Why? Let's visualize: Subtracting the two, the entire common prefix cancels out, leaving exactly the sum of nums[l..r]. O(1) query! From O(n) to O(1) — this is a quantum leap. This is the part that confuses beginners the most. Problem : If l=0, we need to compute prefix[0]. Without a leading zero, prefix[0] would be nums[0] instead of 0. Version with leading zero : The leading zero makes "starting at position 0" use the same formula as every other case , eliminating the need for special handling. Goal : Find the sum of nums[l..r] (closed interval, inclusive of both l and r). Subtracting the two: This is exactly the sum of interval [l, r]. prefix[0] = 0 guarantees correctness. This is exactly why prefix must have length n+1 — there must be room for prefix[n]. IndexError: list assignment index out of range — when i=n-1, prefix[i+1] accesses prefix[n], but the array only has n elements (indices 0..n-1). This is an alternative style (common in competitive programming), but it easily accesses prefix[-1] when l=0. With a 2D prefix sum, each query is O(1). Definition : prefix[i][j] stores the sum of the rectangle with top-left at (0,0) and bottom-right at (i-1, j-1) . In other words: prefix[i][j] = the sum of all elements in rows 0..i-1 and columns 0..j-1. Just like 1D, we add an extra ring of leading zeros. Core formula (inclusion-exclusion): Why subtract prefix[i-1][j-1]? Because prefix[i-1][j] and prefix[i][j-1] both include the top-left region, so it gets counted twice. We must subtract it once. The naive approach: each operation traverses [l, r] adding v, costing O(n) per operation . With m operations, total complexity is O(mn). With a difference array: each operation is O(1), restoration is O(n), total O(m + n). Define the difference array diff: Key property : If you add v to every element in nums[l..r], only two positions in the difference array change: Every other position stays the same! Consider the example: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] Add 2 to [1, 3]: Only diff[1] and diff[4] changed! In practice we do not need to "convert to difference, then restore" — we can record all operations in the diff array and restore once at the end. The only prerequisite for binary search to work: the data must be ordered (monotonic). Why can we throw away half? Because the array is ordered: target < middle element -> target must be on the left target > middle element -> target must be on the right target == middle element -> found it Every comparison eliminates half the remaining elements. With 10 elements you need at most 4 steps; with 1 million elements, at most 20 steps. There is a classic saying online: "90% of programmers cannot write a correct binary search." It is an exaggeration, but binary search really is one of the algorithms most prone to bugs. There are three reasons: 1. Too many boundary conditions : left < right or left <= right? 2. How to compute mid : (left + right) // 2 or (left + right + 1) // 2? 3. Which way to shrink : left = mid or left = mid + 1? Combine the three and you get 8 possible variants, most of them wrong. Core idea : the search interval is [left, right] (closed), including both endpoints. Why while left <= right? Because the interval is closed, when left == right there is still one unchecked element inside. The interval is truly empty only when left > right. Why left = mid + 1? Because nums[mid] has already been compared with the target; it is not the answer and can be removed from the search interval. Expression Meaning When to use --- --- --- (left + right) // 2 Round down General purpose left + (right - left) // 2 Round down Avoids overflow (other languages) (left + right + 1) // 2 Round up Finding a right boundary left + (right - left + 1) // 2 Round up Avoids overflow + right boundary All four work in Python (integers never overflow), but rounding down is the default choice you will use most often . Why it happens : after left = mid the interval does not shrink ([0, 1] -> [0, 1]). The fix : left = mid + 1. But if right is also mid, the problem may be on the other side. This is the classic binary-search infinite loop. Cause: when mid rounds down, mid == left (whenever the interval has length 2), and left = mid stops the interval from shrinking. Many optimization problems have this property: If "the answer is x" works Then "the answer is x+1" (a larger answer) must also work That is monotonicity! We can binary-search for the threshold. Typical scenarios: Cutting wood: cut into k pieces, what is the longest each piece can be? Sharing chocolate: k people split it, what is the most each can get? Minimize the maximum: split an array into m segments, what is the smallest possible maximum segment sum? Task : you have n logs with lengths lengths. Cut them into k pieces of equal length and find the largest possible length for each piece. Brute force : try every length from 1 to max(lengths), O(max n). Far too slow. Binary search on the answer : the answer lives in [1, max(lengths)]. For each candidate mid, check whether we can cut at least k pieces. Key observation: If we can cut 7 pieces at length 100 Then we can certainly cut more pieces at length 50 (at least 7) The shorter the piece, the more pieces you get. That is monotonicity. Three ingredients: 1. Search range : the smallest and largest possible answers 2. Feasibility function : check(x) decides whether answer x is feasible 3. Monotonicity : if x works then x-1 also works

Task : an integer array nums was originally ascending, then rotated at some position (the first few elements were moved to the end). It is not sorted overall, but it is "locally sorted." That is exactly what we can exploit. Property of a rotated array : if you cut it at the middle, at least one of [left, mid] and [mid, right] is fully sorted. Use whichever half is sorted to make the decision. 1. Take mid = (left + right) // 2 2. Decide which half is sorted 3. In the sorted half, check whether target is in range If it is in range -> search that half If not -> search the other half nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3], looking for target = 2: Looking for target = 6: Intuition : a rotated array is an ordered array with "one cut" then reassembled. After one cut, one segment must remain a complete ascending sequence. No matter where you cut, one segment is always a contiguous ascending sequence . The algorithm uses that sorted segment every time to shrink the search range. Time O(log n) -- the same as standard binary search; half the candidates are eliminated each step. In Python, a string cannot be modified once it has been created. There is no such operation as s[0] = "H". If you want to change something, you have to build a brand-new string. Every "modification" of a string actually creates a new string. The problem scenario : concatenating strings over and over inside a loop. What happens on each s += str(i)? 1. Allocate a new block of memory (of length len(s) + 1) 2. Copy every character of s into it 3. Append str(i) at the end 4. Throw away the old s The i-th operation copies i characters. Total copies = 0 + 1 + 2 + ... + (n-1) = O(n²) . Approximate output: The += version grows roughly 4x each step (O(n²)); the join version grows roughly 2x (O(n)). How join works: 1. Walk through all the strings first and compute the total length 2. Allocate one big enough block of memory in a single shot 3. Copy every string into it Total copies = number of all characters = O(n) (linear). Given a string s, find the longest substring that is a palindrome. A substring is any contiguous segment of the original string — you cannot rearrange the characters. Idea : try every possible substring, check whether it is a palindrome, and keep the longest one. How slow is this? Number of substrings: O(n²) Checking each one with == sub[::-1]: O(n) per check Total: O(n³) time That is too slow for any reasonably long string. We can do better. Observation : if you already know that s[i+1:j] is a palindrome, then s[i:j+1] is a palindrome if and only if s[i] == s[j]. Complexity : O(n²) time and O(n²) space. Better than O(n³), but can we drop the space? Key insight : every palindrome has a center . From that center you can expand outward as long as the characters match. Odd-length palindromes ("racecar") have a center character Even-length palindromes ("abba") have a center between two characters Walking through s = "babad", i = 1 (the 'a'): So at i=1 the best we found is "bab" of length 3. How does a computer execute recursion? With something called the call stack . Every time a function is called, the system pushes a frame onto the stack containing the function's parameters, local variables, and which line it is executing. Until the function finishes, its frame stays on the stack. Take factorial(4) as an example: This is "unwind": first it keeps pushing downward (expansion), then after reaching the base case it pops back upward (reduction). The depth of the stack is the depth of the recursion. Factorial n! pushes n frames. The deepest chain of Fibonacci fib(n) is also n frames deep. Key point: stack frames consume memory. Each layer keeps its own local variables and return address. That is why recursion has a space cost — it is not "free," it eats the stack. The most effective low-tech way to see the order of recursion is print + indentation . The indentation equals the recursion depth, so at a glance you know "which layer am I drilling into now." Every recursive call pushes a frame onto the call stack. The stack has a finite size — Python's default maximum is 1000 frames. This means any input whose recursion depth exceeds 1000 will blow up right in your face. factorial(2000) only needs 2000 multiplications, and the amount of computation is perfectly fine. It blows up purely because the stack is not deep enough. This kind of scenario is far too common in practice: processing a file with tens of thousands of lines, traversing a very deep tree, or parsing a very deep JSON. The data itself is fine; the depth of the recursion kills it. Python leaves a back door: Does this solve RecursionError? Yes — but it only pushes the explosion a little further into the future. Even worse: if you set it too high, say setrecursionlimit(10000000), the program does not report an error — it just crashes directly with a Segmentation fault — Python's exception handling never even gets a chance to intervene before the process is gone. Why this is wrong: setrecursionlimit only raises the threshold for Python's own check; it does not actually allocate more memory for the stack. Stack space is given by the operating system and is usually only a few MB

Every heap operation — insert, delete, sink, swim — locates parents and children in the array using these two formulas, with no pointer manipulation involved. In a max-heap, every parent's value is ≥ both of its children's values. In a min-heap, every parent's value is ≤ both of its children's values. The root of a heap is the global maximum (or minimum) element, accessible in O(1). This is the core value of a heap. A heap is "partially ordered," not "fully ordered." A parent ≥ its children, but there is no size relationship between left and right siblings. So a heap cannot do binary search the way a BST can (finding a specific value takes O(n)). Sorting is fundamentally about identifying which of the n! possible permutations the input corresponds to. When n elements are all distinct, their permutations number n! = n × (n−1) × (n−2) × … × 1. The input array is just one of those n! permutations. The job of a sorting algorithm is to "recognize" which one it is. Any sorting algorithm's output must distinguish among all n! possible inputs. If two different inputs produce the same output after running the algorithm, the algorithm must have sorted one of them incorrectly — because it cannot tell those two inputs apart. A "comparison" carries very little information: it has only two outcomes, greater than or less than/equal. One comparison can reduce the "remaining possible permutations" by at most half. To uniquely identify one out of n! possibilities, there must be enough comparisons to keep splitting n! in half until only one remains. That is the entire core of the lower-bound story. Now let us draw it as a decision tree. A decision tree is a binary tree where each internal node represents a "compare a[i] and a[j]", the two edges represent the outcomes "<" and "≥", and each leaf represents a final permutation (output order). The core idea of bubble sort: each pass compares adjacent elements from start to finish, "bubbling" the maximum value of the unsorted portion to the end. After each pass, the last i elements are already sorted. Pass 1 places the maximum at a[n-1], pass 2 places the second-largest at a[n-2], and so on. The comparison count is fixed at n(n-1)/2, regardless of whether the input is sorted. This is bubble sort's biggest waste — even when the data is already sorted, it still foolishly completes every pass. The core idea of selection sort: each pass finds the minimum value in the unsorted portion and places it at the end of the sorted portion. Selection sort swaps at most n−1 times, far fewer than bubble sort. Bubble sort may swap on every single comparison (up to n² swaps in the worst case), while selection sort swaps only once per pass. But selection sort can never "finish early". No matter how sorted the data is, it must scan the entire unsorted portion to determine the minimum. The core idea of insertion sort: maintain a sorted prefix and "insert" the next element into its correct position within that prefix. Insertion sort's inner loop "shifts elements", not "swaps". Heap sort has two steps: 1) build a heap (turn the array into a max-heap); 2) repeatedly extract the maximum from the heap top and place it at the end. Building the heap takes O(n), and n extractions each take O(log n) = O(n log n). Space is O(1) (in-place). Why is building a heap O(n)? At first glance, heapify is O(log n) and there are n/2 nodes to heapify… but the actual total is O(n). Because at level k there are n/2^(k+1) nodes, each sinking at most k levels, total work = Σ k · n/2^(k+1) = O(n). But its cache performance is poor — parent and child nodes are far apart in the array, unlike quick sort's locality. The most common heap bug: miscalculating the left and right child indices. For a 0-based heap, node i's left child is 2i+1, right child is 2i+2, and parent is (i-1)//2. The Fibonacci sequence is defined simply: F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2). The most intuitive implementation is recursive: This implementation has time complexity O(2ⁿ). Why? The recursion tree makes it crystal clear: fib(3) is computed twice, fib(2) is computed three times—the deeper you go, the more repetition. This is overlapping subproblems : the same subproblem is solved over and over. Since subproblems reappear, compute them once and store the result for lookup next time. This is "memoization": Time complexity drops from O(2ⁿ) to O(n). Each fib(k) is computed exactly once; there are n distinct subproblems, each costing O(1). Space complexity is also O(n) (recursion stack + memo table). The three steps of memoization: 1. Define a "memo" (dictionary or array) 2. At the start of the function, check the table—if found, return immediately 3. After computing, store the result in the table If memoization is top-down, can we flip it—start from the smallest subproblems and work our way up? Absolutely. All houses in the same street are connected in a circle—wait, no, they're in a line. Adjacent houses have security systems connected, and if you rob two adjacent houses on the same night, the police will be alerted. Execution trace (nums = [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]): The answer is 12: rob house 0 (2) + house 2 (9) + house 4 (1) = 12. Problem description: You have a knapsack with capacity W and n items. Item i has weight weight[i] and value value[i]. Each item can be chosen at most once. Find the maximum total value you can carry. The classic 0/1 knapsack uses a 2D dp: For the i-th item (1-indexed), there are two choices: Notice that dp[i][j] only depends on dp[i-1][...] (the previous row), so we can use a 1D array with rolling optimization: This is the core of the lesson. The meaning of the 1D dp[j]: dp[j] = the maximum value achievable with a knapsack of capacity j (in the current state). When considering the i-th item, updating dp[j] requires the "previous round's" value of dp[j - weights[i]]. Forward order (j从小到大) : when updating dp[j], dp[j - weights[i]] may have already been updated in this round → meaning item i was used more than once Reverse order (j从大到小) : when updating dp[j], dp[j - weights[i]] hasn't been updated yet this round → guarantees item i is used only once In one sentence: reverse order guarantees that dp[j - w] is the "previous round's" value; forward order causes the "current round's" value to be reused → item selected repeatedly. The only difference between Unbounded Knapsack and 0/1 Knap

The greedy approach: at each step, make the locally optimal choice, hoping it leads to the globally optimal result. Sounds great, but the key question is: does greedy actually guarantee the global optimum? Answer: not always. Greedy is only correct when the problem satisfies the "greedy choice property." In other words: if you pick the "best option right now," and no matter how you arrange things afterward, you can never do better than "not picking this option," then greedy works. Problem: You have a set of activities, each with a start time and an end time. Only one activity can run at a time. What's the maximum number of activities you can attend? Greedy strategy: always pick the activity with the earliest end time. Why does greedy work? Intuition: The earlier an activity ends, the more time remains for subsequent activities. Picking the earliest-ending activity doesn't shrink your options for what comes next. Formal proof (exchange argument): Suppose the optimal solution's first activity is A, and the earliest-ending activity is B (B ends no later than A). First, let's review what each tool solves: Tool Core problem it solves --- --- Prefix sums Range sum queries: reduces O(n) range queries to O(1) Hash table Fast lookup: O(1) to check "exists?" or "where?" Sliding window Two pointers maintain a window: O(n) to process "subarrays satisfying a condition" The core idea behind combining them: Problem: Given an integer array nums and a target value k, find the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k. Brute force O(n²): enumerate all start and end positions, compute the sum. O(n²), guaranteed TLE at n=10⁵. Prefix sum prefix[i] = nums[0] + ... + nums[i-1]. The sum of subarray nums[j..i-1] = prefix[i] - prefix[j]. We want prefix[i] - prefix[j] == k, i.e., prefix[j] == prefix[i] - k. Use a hash table to record how many times each prefix sum has appeared. While iterating, look up how many times prefix[i] - k has appeared. Time complexity O(n), space O(n). Problem: Given an array of positive integers and an integer S, find the length of the shortest contiguous subarray with sum ≥ S. Since the array is all positive, the window sum is monotonic: expanding increases the sum, shrinking decreases it. This makes sliding window applicable.

Problem: Given an integer array nums, find a contiguous subarray with the largest sum (a subarray must contain at least one element), and return that maximum sum. Example: Why this problem? It's simple enough for anyone to understand, yet rich enough to have 4 solution approaches, from O(n³) to O(n). Walking through all of them, you'll experience how "optimization" happens step by step. The most naive approach: enumerate all possible start and end positions of subarrays, summing each one. Complexity O(n³). At n=10⁴, it's unusable. What's the problem? The innermost loop recomputes the sum from i to j every time, doing massive redundant work. Optimization idea: enumerate start i, then expand end j while accumulating, avoiding recomputation. Complexity O(n²). Better than O(n³), but still TLE at n=10⁵. Further: use prefix sums to reduce sum queries to O(1). Still O(n²), just with a smaller constant. Can we do better? Divide-and-conquer idea: the maximum subarray is either in the left half, the right half, or crosses the midpoint. Complexity O(n log n). Recursion depth is log n, each level does O(n) work. In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe constructed four artificial datasets, now known as Anscombe's quartet . Each set contains 11 points, each point an (x, y) pair. The x's and y's of these four datasets have basically the same summary statistics . Means, variances, correlation, regression slope — identical across all four. If you only report those numbers, no one can tell the datasets apart. The four pictures tell four completely different stories: Dataset What it looks like What the story is --- --- --- I Ordinary scatter, roughly a straight line Classic positive correlation: bigger x, bigger y II One clean curve Non-linear relationship — fitting a line is wrong III All points but one sit on a near-vertical line An extreme value dominates everything; the slope is an illusion IV All x's identical except for one outlier Again outlier-dominated ; remove it and there is nothing left Statistics compress data, and compression loses information. Means, variances and correlations collapse 11 points into 4 numbers, necessarily discarding shape. The regression line is the line with slope 0.5 , but it only makes sense for dataset I. A histogram slices a continuous variable into intervals (bins) and counts how many records fall into each one. It is the most basic tool for inspecting a distribution. bins=20 is the number of intervals . More bins make each bar narrower, exposing local fluctuations but also the random jitter of the sample; fewer bins make the curve smoother but can merge two peaks into one. This is not "more is better", it is a parameter you tune by trying values. Crash site 1: too many bins, noise mistaken for structure. With only 244 records split into 60 intervals, many bars hold 0 or 1 record, and the result looks like a sawtooth. You would be tempted to see a cycle where none exists. Each interval needs enough records , so as a rule of thumb start between bins = sqrt(n) and n/10; for n=244 that means roughly 15 to 25. A histogram is sensitive to bin boundaries, the shape changes if you shift them slightly. KDE (kernel density estimation) avoids that with a smooth curve, which is better for seeing the overall centre and spread . fill=True fills the area under the curve, making it read more like "area = probability". Ubuntu's apt and several macOS system tools depend on it. Every package you install or upgrade there is like moving the furniture in someone else's house. Crash Site: upgrading a system package breaks a system command What you see: the system's own apt command crashes because a dependency you upgraded became incompatible. Fixing it costs an hour that should never have existed. The more subtle problem is dependency conflict . Project A needs requests==2.28, project B needs requests==2.31. This creates a .venv/ folder containing an independent copy of the Python interpreter and an empty site-packages. pip is Python's official package installer: stable and reliable, but slow. The slowness lives in two places: 1. Dependency resolution — given a list of requirements, pip must find mutually compatible versions for every package. That solver runs in Python, and on a complex project it can take tens of seconds. 2. Installation — download the wheel, unpack it, compile it (if no prebuilt wheel exists), and copy it into site-packages. Packages are processed one at a time. Neither bottleneck is pip being lazy; both are consequences of its design. So the community built faster tools. uv is a Python package manager and project manager written in Rust by Astral — the same team behind Ruff. Its headline is speed: official benchmarks put it 10–100× faster than pip. Where the speed comes from: Dependency resolution in Rust — the same solving problem finishes in milliseconds instead of tens of seconds. Parallel downloads and installs — unlike pip's serial pipeline. A global package cache — different projects share one cache directory, so an already-downloaded package is never fetched twice. Built-in virtual environment management — no need to python -m venv first and then activate. Notice that u

Flat layout — every source file sits at the project root. src layout — source code lives under one src/ directory. The difference is not aesthetics; it changes how tests behave. Under flat layout, tests/ sits at the same level as the source. When you run tests, Python starts from the root, so import main works immediately. The problem: tests exercise the source on disk, not the installed package. If you forget to include a file in the package, the tests still pass — because they never went through the installation path. The src layout forces you to install the package first (pip install -e .), so tests import the installed version. Local testing and real usage now follow the same path, and a missing file surfaces during testing. tests/ is not just "a folder for test files." It sends a signal: this project has tests, and they live separately from the code under test. Name each test file after its target module (test xxx.py tests xxx.py) and the mapping is obvious at a glance. Because test files live in tests/, imports look like from myproject import user — identical to how a user would import — which is precisely why the src layout is the stricter choice. A good name meets three standards: it says what the thing is, what it does, and what unit it is in. Stating the unit matters especially. Is a timeout in seconds or milliseconds? A disciplined team makes the choice explicit: See the name and you know the unit — no documentation dive, no guesswork. In most fonts, the lowercase letter l, the uppercase letter O, and the uppercase letter I look almost identical to the digits 1, 0, and 1. Crash Site: l and 1 get confused and produce a bug What you see: NameError: name 'l' is not defined. You meant to pass the list, but you typed l — which looks like 1, and also like the first letter of items. Three days later you cannot tell the difference yourself. PEP 8, Python's official style guide, explicitly advises: never use l, O, or I as single-character variable names. Use i, j, k for loop counters; call a list lst or, better, use the plural noun items. A boolean name should answer "yes or no" directly. The three prefixes is , has , and can eliminate a great deal of ambiguity. Newcomers stop guessing. The fix: stage precisely, or use the interactive form git add -p (-p for patch) asks you chunk by chunk "do you want this hunk staged?" — finer-grained than files, and invaluable when you changed two things in one file but only want to commit one of them. Three days later you want to revert "the login logic change," but it is tangled with the reformatting and the README in the same commit. You cannot revert the login portion alone — granularity this coarse destroys the value of version control. A good commit does exactly one thing, and that one thing fits in the subject line. main (or master) should always be in a usable, deployable state. That is both a team convention and an assumption made by your automation. Crash Site: an urgent bug arrives while you are halfway through editing main What you see: the checkout is blocked because the working tree has uncommitted changes. You are forced to either commit a half-finished state to main or stash it. Either way, main is polluted. The fix: branch off main, then edit Your half-finished work lives on feature/phone-login; main stays clean. When the urgent bug arrives, just switch back to main and open a hotfix branch. The standard flow: Branch names conventionally carry a prefix and a purpose : feature/..., fix/..., hotfix/..., refactor/... — matching the commit types. Two ways to integrate a branch into main. Merge — preserves the branch history and creates a merge commit. The result: The history faithfully records the development process , but enough forks and it starts to look like spaghetti. Review is not about whether the code runs — CI already verified that. Review is about what lies beyond the code: 1. Design soundness — does this change belong here? Is there a simpler approach? Is it solving at the wrong level of abstraction? 2. Readability — can someone arriving six months from now understand it? Do the names, comments, and structure explain themselves? 3. Test coverage — are the boundaries covered? Are error paths tested? Did changing the logic come with updated tests? 4. Impact on existing code — could this break another module? Did it touch a public API? 5. Security and configuration — any hardcoded secrets? Is input validated? Are permission checks complete? Separate "must change" from "open for discussion" GitHub / GitLab support marking with prefixes: blocking: or must: — must be resolved before merging. nit: — a nitpick, may be ignored. question: — a question, not a request for change. 3. The test pyramid has three layers. From top to bottom the count drops, the speed rises, and the ability to pinpoint a failure falls. Layer Owns Speed Share Typical tools --- --- --- --- --- End-to-end (E2E) The whole system wired together works seconds to minutes at most 10% Selenium, Playwright Integration modules connect (database, network, filesystem) milliseconds to seconds 20% 30% pytest + a real database Unit one function or one class behaves correctly microseconds 60% 80% pytest + unittest Unit tests cover a single function or method. No database, no network, no file reads. They are the fastest and the easiest to pin down — when one fails, you know exactly which function is wrong. Integration tests verify that "my code works together with the real dependency." For example: after the order service writes to PostgreSQL, can it read the row back? Does a published message actually get consumed? They are allowed to use a real database, but they do not start the whole web service. End-to-end tests walk the full flow from the user's perspective: open the browser → log in → place an order → pay → see the order. They are closest to reality, but also slow, brittle, and hard to diagnos

A fixture is pytest's dependency-injection mechanism. A test function names a fixture in its parameters and pytest calls it automatically, passing the result in. sample users is never written out by hand in every test — pytest injects it. The test only says "what data do I need," not "where does that data come from." Fixture scope : by default the fixture re-runs once per test function (function). There is also module (once per module) and session (once per test session). An expensive resource like a database connection belongs at session scope so you avoid reconnecting over and over. The code before yield is the setup, the code after it is the teardown. This is the standard pytest idiom for "cleanup." The dumbest way to test ten input/output pairs is to copy the test function ten times. @pytest.mark.parametrize generates separate test cases from one list of inputs. After running, you get 8 independent cases, each passing or failing on its own, so you can see at a glance which input broke. When several test modules need the same fixture, do not copy and paste. Three kinds of dependency must be isolated: 1. Uncontrollable dependencies — network requests, third-party APIs, the system clock. You do not own them, and you cannot guarantee they are online or returning consistent results. 2. Side-effecting dependencies — sending email, charging a card, writing a file. You cannot actually send an email on every test run. 3. Slow dependencies — a real database call takes dozens of milliseconds; times 1,000 tests, that is half a minute. Crash site: a test that really makes an HTTP request Every now and then CI's network jitters and the test fails at random. And this test is checking "is the network up," not "is my code correct." The fix: mock requests.get and verify how it was called Now the test depends only on get user name's logic, not on the network. pytest's built-in monkeypatch fixture is designed for temporarily replacing attributes, environment variables, and dict entries, then restoring them automatically when the test ends. The advantage of monkeypatch is automatic restoration : when the test ends, the patched attribute is restored, so it cannot pollute other tests. Mocking has a cost. Line coverage answers one question: was each line of code executed at least once ? It does not answer "did it produce the right result?" This test drives divide's coverage close to 100% — the normal branch runs — but it never touches the b == 0 exception branch. Any caller passing b=0 crashes, and you never knew. Use the coverage tool with pytest to generate a report: The -m flag lists the uncovered line numbers in the Missing column, which is the most valuable part of the report. Counterexample 1: code ran, but nothing was asserted Coverage is 100%, but nothing is verified. If the function returns None, the tests still go green. Counterexample 2: boundaries were never tested Only 500 was tested. The boundaries 499 (returns 0) and 1000 (returns 0.2) were never touched. Full coverage, boundary bug still present. Counterexample 3: exception paths were never tested Only the "file exists" path is tested, so the exception branch is uncovered. In production, when the config file is missing, that behavior was never validated. Crash site: coverage used as a KPI The moment coverage becomes a hard metric, people game it — and that is not coverage's fault, it is the wrong target being measure

CI (Continuous Integration) boils down to one idea: integrate code into the main branch frequently, and verify it automatically on every integration. Its value is not speed; it is that every commit runs the same checks, and everyone gets the same result. Crash site: passes locally, fails in CI Cause: the author installed requests but never added it to requirements.txt, so it existed locally but was absent in CI's clean environment. Crash site: forgot to run the tests CI solves "inconsistent verification standards": local environments differ wildly, but CI is one clean machine, one set of commands, one result. When it passes, others can pull with confidence. GitHub Actions configuration lives in .github/workflows/ as YAML. A few key concepts : on: when to run. Common triggers are push and pull request; you can also run on a schedule. jobs: a workflow can have several jobs, which run in parallel by default. Here there is only lint-and-test. runs-on: which machine. ubuntu-latest is the most common; there is also windows-latest and macos-latest. steps: the ordered sequence. uses references an existing action; run executes a shell command. actions/checkout@v4: almost always the first st

Semantic Versioning (SemVer) uses the format MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, for example 2.13.7. PATCH — a backward-compatible bug fix . No interface changes, no semantic behavior changes, just a bug fixed. MINOR — a backward-compatible addition . New functionality, new parameters (with defaults), new modules, while old code still works. MAJOR — an incompatible API change . A function was removed, a parameter order changed, a return type changed, or the semantic behavior changed. Crash site: promoting a bug fix to a major version Consequence : users see the major bump and assume you introduced a breaking change, so they do not upgrade. A "trivial" release slows the ecosystem's adoption of your library. The version number stops carrying signal. The test is simple: can existing users keep working without changing a single line of code after they upgrade? Change Breaking? --- --- Adding a function, adding an optional parameter (with a default) no Fixing a bug (including making a "wrong" behavior correct) no (it is a patch, unless users depended on the bug) Renaming a function yes Removing a function or a parameter yes Changing a parameter order or its default yes Changing a return type or a field

A wheel installs an order of magnitude faster and does not require the user to have a C compiler. The classic development argument is an environment mismatch: Three machines, three Python versions, three results. The issue is not who is right; it is that the code was never bound to its environment . Docker's answer: package the application with everything it needs — operating system, Python interpreter, libraries, environment variables — into an image , then run that image anywhere Docker is installed and get the same container every time. An image = a packaged "template," like an ISO installer; it is a static file. A container = an "instance" of that image, like a machine installed from the disc; it is a running process. One image can start any number of containers. A container that runs on your laptop behaves identically when dropped into CI or onto a server. Crash site: assuming "Docker means consistent environments" Consequence : latest is a floating tag, so every build can pull a different version. The image that builds today may fail to build tomorrow, or behave differently. The environment only looks consistent. A useful analogy: image is to container as class is to object. Key concepts: 1. The README is the front door of your project, the first thing anyone sees when they open the repository. A solid open-source README has these sections, in order: 1. Project introduction : one sentence on what it does, what problem it solves, and who it is for. 2. Installation : the complete path from zero to running, including the Python version, dependency installation, and any system-level dependencies. 3. Quick start / usage example : the smallest runnable example, ideally copy-pasteable. 4. Configuration : environment variables, config files, what the user must supply. 5. Basic usage : common operations, CLI flags, API entry points. 6. How to contribute : branch conventions, the PR flow, code style, whether to open an issue first. 7. Testing and development : how to run tests and set up a dev environment. 8. License : which license you chose. When a program is slow, human intuition is almost always wrong. You stare at an "ugly-looking" loop, spend two hours rewriting it, and discover the real bottleneck was somewhere else — a database query, a full table scan, a function called in a loop. That is what "premature optimization is the root of all evil" really means: before you know where the bottleneck is, any optimization is a gamble. Worse, optimized code is often harder to read and easier to break. Trading 1% performance for 20% readability is usually a bad deal. So the correct order is: 1. Measure — run a profile and get real data. 2. Locate — find the function or line that takes the most time. 3. Optimize — change only the hotspot, and change one thing at a time to verify it. 4. Measure again — run it again to confirm it actually got faster. Crash site: guessing the wrong target Lesson : after measuring, you find that most of the time goes where few people expect. Profile before optimizing — it is discipline, not a suggestion. timeit compares which of two small code blocks is faster. It runs the code many times automatically and averages the result, filtering out system noise. Do not use time.time() to time things by

print is a great helper during development, but in production it has three fatal flaws: 1. No levels — there is no way to tell whether this is debug info or a fatal error; it all blends together. 2. No context — you know "something failed," but which request, which user, what parameters? Nobody knows. 3. Not searchable — once the log volume grows, reading text by eye is the same as not logging at all. When production breaks, your investigation path is: alert → locate the service → filter logs by time or request ID → reconstruct what happened. Every step of that path depends on structured, contextual logs. Python's standard library ships logging, which is enough — no extra install required: "A line of plain text" is comfortable for human eyes but hard for machines to parse. Structured logs (typically one JSON object per line) have one big advantage: you can filter, aggregate, and graph them by field. Output: Crash site: cramming everything into the message string The fix : pass structured fields via extra={} and put only the event name in the message. "Filter by user id" then becomes an exact query instead of a full-text regex. This is the most important rule in the lesson. Logs lan

Your own code may have no holes, but the third-party libraries you pull in do. log4shell in 2021 and various supply-chain incidents in 2024 all make the same point: your dependency tree is part of your attack surface. The good news is that scanning for dependency vulnerabilities costs almost nothing. pip-audit is the officially recommended dependency vulnerability scanner, backed by the vulnerability database of the Python Software Packaging Authority: Sample output: Crash site: never scanning until the security team reports it The fix : wire pip-audit into CI so it becomes a hard gate, just like "run the tests." Vulnerabilities must be fixed before merging or releasing. Hardcoding secrets is the single worst security mistake. Once a secret is in code or version control, it gets copied into clones, forks, CI caches, and history — and is nearly impossible to erase completely. The minimum acceptable approach is environment variables : Pair this with a .env file ( which must be in .gitignore ): Load .env with python-dotenv: The more proper approach is a secret manager (KMS / Secret Manager) , such as the services cloud providers offer. Running a script locally means you type a command in a terminal, watch the output, and handle errors on the spot. A production service is completely different: nobody is watching, it crashes on its own, it must restart on its own, and it must serve many requests at once. Dimension Local Production --- --- --- Startup typed by hand a process manager starts it automatically Crash you see the error automatic restart + alert Configuration hardcoded in code environment variables / config center Logs terminal output written to disk + collected centrally Health checks unnecessary required, so the load balancer can decide Rollback manual git checkout one-click switch to the previous version Resources sole use of your machine constrained, resource usage must be monitored Crash site: thinking python app.py is deployment The fix : use a process manager (systemd, supervisor) or an orchestrator (Docker Compose, K8s) to host the process, ensuring it restarts on crash and starts on boot. Two of the most common setups: systemd (the standard on Linux servers) Containers (Docker Compose) Crash site: the wrong restart policy Lesson : restart: on-failure / unless-stopped is safer than always; pair it

Geometry management = deciding where each widget is and how large it is. Without a geometry manager in tkinter, the widget is invisible. The three geometry managers: Manager Name Idea One-line verdict --- --- --- --- pack() Packing Line up against an edge Simple, but no precise positioning grid() Grid Place by row and column like a table Most common, most flexible place() Placing Specify absolute/relative coordinates Most free, and most chaotic The three managers must not be mixed on the same parent (crucial — see the crash scene later). They can, however, each be used on different parents. pack's logic is "pick a direction, hug that edge, and line up in turn." The three Labels line up from top to bottom by default (the default side is "top"). pack's arguments: Argument Purpose --- --- side Which edge to hug: "top"/"bottom"/"left"/"right" fill Stretch along which axis: "x"/"y"/"both"/"none" expand Whether to claim extra space: True/False padx / pady External margin (between widgets) ipadx / ipady Internal padding (empty space inside the widget) anchor Which side of its allocated space to hug: "n"/"s"/"e"/"w"/"center" When pack is a good fit: a toolbar with a row or column of button

pack defaults to side="top", stacking widgets top to bottom: The three Labels each occupy their own row from top to bottom. This is pack at its most intuitive. side decides which edge of the parent the widget hugs: A practical "top + bottom + left + middle" layout: The order of the side arguments affects the final layout — pack allocates space to each widget "in the order it is called." For complex structures, the recommended approach is Frame partitioning with pack inside each Frame. fill lets a widget expand when extra space is available: Value Effect --- --- "none" Keep the natural size (default) "x" Fill horizontally "y" Fill vertically "both" Fill in both directions The first Label stretches across the full window width; the second keeps its natural text width. Compare the effect of different fill values: Only fill="x" or fill="both" causes the widget to grow wider as the window grows. expand=True means "if there is leftover space, give me a share." It is often paired with fill: The red Label claims all the space not taken by the blue Label. The difference between expand and fill: expand decides "do I want space?", while fill decides "now that I have space, how do I use it?" W

grid treats the parent as a table. Each widget specifies which cell it occupies using row and column, both starting from 0. The result is a tidy two-row, two-column form. The labels sit in the left column, the input boxes in the right column, and the two columns align vertically. This is grid's core value: alignment. pack cannot align columns; grid supports it natively. You can skip row and column numbers rather than using 0, 1, 2 in sequence: Empty rows still occupy space (very little, but it is there). In practice you usually lay things out in order; skipping numbers is mainly useful for "reserving an area." A widget can occupy more than one cell. columnspan=2 means "occupy two columns horizontally": "Heading" spans both columns, behaving like a table header. rowspan means "span rows vertically": "Sidebar" spans 3 rows, acting like a side panel. sticky decides which direction the widget hugs inside its cell and whether it fills the cell. Value Effect --- --- "" (default) Centered, natural size "w" Hug the left side "e" Hug the right side "n" Hug the top "s" Hug the bottom "ew" Fill horizontally "ns" Fill vertically "nsew" Fill in all four directions sticky is the most underrated

First, reproduce this classic problem: After running it, drag the window from 400x300 to 800x600 — and the widgets stay crammed in the top-left corner while the empty space on the right keeps growing. This is the "widgets will not move" problem. grid treats space allocation as a "dividing the cake" problem. When the window grows, who gets the extra cake? By default, nobody — every weight is 0 — so the widgets keep their original sizes and the leftover space is dumped on the right and bottom edges. The fix: use columnconfigure and rowconfigure to tell grid "this column/row has weight and wants a share of the cake." Now, when you enlarge the window: column 1 (where the input boxes are) grows wider, and row 2 (where the button is) grows taller. weight decides "how the extra space is divided." It is an integer: Situation Allocation result --- --- Every row/column has weight 0 Nobody wants space; leftover is dumped on the right/bottom Only one column has weight=1 That column takes all the extra space One column has weight=1, another weight=2 The second column gets twice as much space as the first Two columns both have weight=1 The two columns split the space evenly Weight is a ratio, no

The actual string is still there untouched — show only changes what the screen draws. This is exactly how every password field on the web works. The value is never altered; only its visual representation is masked. Three states, three different behaviours: Read-only is perfect for a result field.
