Text is a multiline editing widget — the big blank area in Notepad is a Text. It looks like a taller Entry, but the similarity ends there. Text manages paragraphs, wrapping, selection, and styles all on its own. The arguments you'll reach for most: Argument What it does --- --- width / height Width in characters / height in lines wrap How to wrap long lines: "none" / "char" / "word" state "normal" editable / "disabled" read-only fg / bg Text colour / background colour font The font for the body text spacing1 / spacing2 / spacing3 Space above a line / within wrapped lines / below a line wrap="word" wraps on word boundaries, not in the middle of a word. For Chinese text it wraps on character boundaries. It's almost always the right choice. This is the single most confusing thing about Text: positions are written "line.column", lines start at 1, columns start at 0. Why does the line count start at 1 but the column at 0? Blame Tcl/Tk, tkinter's underlying library — that's just how it was designed in the 1990s. Don't fight it; learn the rule. Try it yourself: The slice goes from column 0 up to, but not including, column 5 — the same half-open logic Python uses for slicing. insert(index,

A Checkbutton is a tick box. Tick as many as you like. Three boxes appear, all clickable — but your program has no idea which ones are ticked. There's no variable binding yet, so the ticks live only on screen. Pass a variable class through variable= and the box becomes readable from code. var.get() returns True or False. Tick the boxes, hit Confirm, and the terminal lists exactly what you picked. The mechanical rule: one variable per box, one if per variable. More boxes means more of both — there's no built-in "give me the list of ticked boxes", which is why Checkbutton groups are usually small. By default a Checkbutton reports True when ticked and False when not. You can change both. A common variant pairs IntVar with onvalue=1, offvalue=0 when the rest of your code expects numbers rather than booleans. A Radiobutton is the round option button. In a group, one selection cancels the others. The two lines that matter: variable is the same object, value is different on every button. Pick Shanghai and var becomes "Shanghai"; pick Guangzhou and it becomes "Guangzhou". The old value is overwritten — that's the whole mechanism of mutual exclusion. Radiobuttons that share a variable form

Listbox shows a list of items the user can pick from, one or many at a time. insert(index, item) adds an item; "end" means append. Five cities, five rows, click any of them. The arguments you'll use most: Argument What it does --- --- selectmode "browse" single (default) / "single" / "multiple" / "extended" multi-select height How many rows are visible width Width in characters fg / bg Text / background colours selectbackground / selectforeground The selection's colours curselection() returns a tuple of selected indexes, counting from 0. In multi-select mode, curselection() returns several indexes: Method Purpose --- --- insert(idx, items) Insert at idx ("end" = tail) delete(first, last=None) Delete one item or a range get(first, last=None) Read one item or a range size() Total number of items curselection() Tuple of selected indexes selection set(first, last=None) Select items from code selection clear(first, last=None) Deselect items activate(idx) Highlight an item selection set and selection clear are Listbox-specific — note the names. They are not select/deselect; those belong to Checkbutton. A long list needs a scrollbar. The catch is that the connection goes in both direction

ttk is tkinter's themed submodule — it draws controls in the native style of your OS. Side by side, the difference is obvious: tkinter widget ttk equivalent --- --- Vintage look, mid-90s aesthetic Native look, current OS tk.Button ttk.Button tk.Label ttk.Label tk.Entry ttk.Entry tk.Checkbutton ttk.Checkbutton tk.Radiobutton ttk.Radiobutton tk.Frame ttk.Frame The rule: use ttk unless you have a reason not to. Reasons not to include wanting exact colours (ttk fights you on those) or needing a feature only the classic widget exposes. Three concrete advantages: 1. It looks modern — rounded corners on macOS, flat design on Windows, native Adwaita on Linux. 2. It adds widgets tkinter lacks : Combobox, Spinbox, Treeview, Notebook, Progressbar, Separator. 3. Themes are switchable through ttk.Style(). Switching themes: clam is the portable one — same look on every OS. vista/xpnative is Windows-only, aqua is macOS-only. When you need screenshots that look identical across machines, clam is the answer. Combobox is "type something or pick from a list" in one widget. values is the list of options; set() reads and writes the current value. Two equivalent ways: cb.get() returns whatever is shown

A callback is a function you hand over to be called later, when something happens. A button's command is the simplest possible example. The sequence: you write the function, the button holds onto it, the user clicks, tkinter calls it. You're not calling say hi yourself anywhere — that's the whole point of a callback. command=say hi is correct; command=say hi() is the mistake everyone makes once. With parentheses, say hi() runs immediately — right there, while the window is still being built. Its return value (None) is what gets handed to command. So the function fires once at startup, and clicking the button does absolutely nothing. The fix is just to delete the parentheses. It's a small character with a dramatic effect, which is why it shows up in nearly every tkinter tutorial. command wants a function object, not the function's name as text. A string has no code to run, and tkinter has no way to know what "greet" was supposed to mean. Form Meaning --- --- command=function name The usual case command=lambda: ... When you need arguments (Lesson 17) command=callable object Any object with a call method Every form has one thing in common: command receives a callable that takes zero a

Here's the trap in its simplest form: command=greet passes nothing, and greet demands a name. Click it and you get missing 1 required positional argument: 'name'. command=greet("Zhang") is wrong too — it calls greet immediately and hands None to command. You need a wrapper: a function with no arguments whose body calls greet("Zhang"). lambda builds a small function on the spot: lambda: greet("Zhang") reads as "a function of no arguments whose body is greet('Zhang')". Click the button and tkinter calls that function, which in turn calls greet("Zhang"). For comparison, the two forms side by side: lambda parameters: expression. The colon must be followed by a single expression — something that produces a value. No statements, no blocks. The outer lambda stays argument-free; inside, it can pass any number of arguments to the real function. lambda also captures "which data belongs to which button" — the pattern you'll use constantly: lambda name=f: ... uses a default argument to freeze the current value of f inside the lambda. That default-value trick is the key to everything in this lesson. partial also bakes arguments into a function: partial(greet, "Zhang") returns a new callable tha

bind connects an event sequence to a callback. When the event happens, tkinter calls your function and hands it an event object. Click anywhere in the window and the terminal shows the coordinates. Button-1 is the left button; event.x and event.y are measured from the top-left corner of whatever you bound to. A sequence is a string: <modifier-type-detail>. The common event types: Type Meaning --- --- Button-1 / 2 / 3 Left / middle / right button pressed ButtonRelease-1 Left button released Motion Mouse moved Enter / Leave Mouse entered / left the widget Key / KeyPress A key was pressed KeyRelease A key was released FocusIn / FocusOut Widget gained / lost focus Configure Widget was resized or repositioned Destroy Widget is being destroyed Bind to a widget and only that widget triggers the callback. Bind to root and the whole window listens. The difference is reach. A widget-level binding is precise — the mouse must be over that button. A root binding catches everything the window receives. Pick the narrower scope that does the job; a global key binding can interfere with text entry if you're not careful. tkinter passes an event object whether you want it or not. It carries everythin

Keyboard events are delivered only to the widget that currently has focus — the one with the blinking cursor. At startup one of the entries holds focus (usually the first). Click the other and focus moves there. Only the focused widget receives keystrokes — that's why typing into a form fills one field at a time. focus set() moves focus to a widget; focus get() asks root which widget has it. focus set() is the single most useful trick in this lesson. Use it on the main input field during init so the user can start typing immediately instead of having to click first. Bind the modifier plus the key, then call the function from the callback. <Control-s> means Ctrl+S. The event=None default deserves a closer look. The same save works as a bind callback (tkinter passes an event) and as a plain function call from a menu — the parameter becomes optional. Write your file-handling functions this way and they slot into either mechanism. The conventions users expect: Shortcut Usual meaning --- --- Ctrl+N New Ctrl+O Open Ctrl+S Save Ctrl+Shift+S Save As Ctrl+Z Undo Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V Copy / Paste Delete Delete F5 Refresh Esc Cancel / close Return "break" to swallow an event and stop it reaching t

trace is a notification system on tkinter's variable classes. When the variable changes, your function runs. var.trace("w", on change) says: call on change whenever this variable is written to. Set the value and the print appears immediately, with no button and no event binding. Mode When it fires --- --- "r" The variable was read "w" The variable was written to "u" The variable was deleted (unset) "w" is the one you'll reach for. Reading and deletion traces have niche uses (debugging, resource cleanup); the live-update pattern is always write. tkinter passes three arguments to a trace callback: name, index, and mode — though the exact form varies between tkinter versions, so the safe play is args. If you only care about the value, keep it simple: args absorbs whatever tkinter hands over and keeps your code working across versions. This is the form to memorise. Two inputs, one result, no button — the answer appears as you type. v1.trace("w", calc) and v2.trace("w", calc) — every change to either input reruns calc. Type 12 in the first box and the result column shows 12 plus whatever's in the second. The or 0 is deliberate. An empty StringVar is "", and float("") raises ValueError.

A pop-up pauses the flow and forces attention; that's exactly why you should use it sparingly. In a command-line program you print a message and hope the user sees it. In a GUI the user might not even be looking at the terminal. A messagebox puts a small window in front of everything else with a message and a couple of buttons, so the user has to deal with it. Run this and click the button: a new little window appears with an information icon, your title, your text, and an OK button. Click OK and it goes away. That's the whole pattern — a function call that blocks until the user responds. showinfo, showwarning, and showerror all work the same way; only the icon and tone change. Function Icon shown Typical use --- --- --- showinfo(title, msg) blue "i" "File saved successfully" showwarning(title, msg) yellow "!" "You have unsaved changes" showerror(title, msg) red "X" "Could not open the file" showinfo with parent= any attach to a specific window The second argument is the message body and \n produces a line break, so you can write a short paragraph. Don't pour a stack trace in there — the user doesn't want to read one and you don't want to expose internal details. One or two sentenc

askopenfilename shows the standard Open dialog and returns the full path the user chose, or an empty string if they cancelled. That string is all you need to read the file with Python's normal file tools. Click Open, browse to a file, click OK, and the path lands in your variable. Cancel or close the dialog and you get ''. That empty string is your signal that nothing was chosen, so check for it before you try to open anything. The dialog only picks the path; opening and reading the file is still your job. Text.delete("1.0", tk.END) clears the widget first so you don't paste new content on top of the old. Then insert("1.0", ...) puts the fresh text at the very start. That two-step clear-and-insert is the standard way to reload a Text widget. When the user cancels, path is ''. Passing that to open() raises FileNotFoundError — a confusing error for the user, who thought they were just closing the dialog. Guard with if not path: return. filetypes decides which files appear in the dialog's dropdown. It's a list of (label, pattern) tuples, and pattern can be a string or a tuple of extensions. The first tuple in the list is the default choice shown in the dropdown. " .txt" matches only f

askstring, askinteger, and askfloat each show a small dialog with a prompt and a single field; they differ only in what they hand you back. Function Returns --- --- askstring(title, prompt) str, or None if cancelled askinteger(title, prompt, ...) int, or None if cancelled askfloat(title, prompt, ...) float, or None if cancelled Type a name, click OK, and name is that string. Click Cancel or the X and it's None. That None is the key difference from a normal Entry widget — you don't need to wire up a Button and read .get(), the dialog does it and returns the answer directly. askinteger and askfloat validate for you: a non-number can't be confirmed. minvalue and maxvalue reject values outside the range and keep the dialog open until the user fixes it. You don't write a try/except for that case — the dialog handles it. Other useful keyword arguments are initialvalue (pre-fills the field) and parent (anchors the dialog to your window). When the user cancels, count is None, and None > 0 raises TypeError. The fix is the same guard you use everywhere else: check for None first, then do the comparison. Without parent, the dialog can appear behind your main window on macOS and some Linux set

A menu is a widget like any other, but it lives in the window's frame rather than being packed. Step 1 creates a Menu attached to root. Step 2 tells the window to display it as the menu bar with root.config(menu=...). Step 3 adds command items — each one is just a labelled button that fires a callback. That's the whole skeleton; everything else is variations on it. You can build the menu perfectly and still see nothing, because root.config(menu=menubar) is the one line that actually puts it on screen. If your menu is "missing", this is the first line to look for. A dropdown is a second Menu that you add to the first one with add cascade instead of add command. add cascade(label=..., menu=...) is the bridge: it puts a labelled item on the bar that, when clicked, reveals the submenu you built. add separator() draws the thin divider line that groups related commands — put it before Quit, before destructive actions, or anywhere it helps readability. A menu built with tearoff=True (the default) has a dotted line at the top that lets the user drag the menu into a floating window of its own. That was useful in the 1990s; today it mostly confuses people and adds an empty first slot you hav

Toplevel(root) creates a new independent window; after that it accepts widgets exactly like root does. Click the button and a brand-new window appears, complete with its own title bar and close button. It runs on the same mainloop, so closing the main window closes everything. Any widget you already know — Label, Entry, Button — can be packed into a Toplevel just as it would be into root. Chaining .title(...) after the constructor is legal but confusing, and it stops working the moment you want to do more with top. The readable pattern is three separate lines: create, configure, populate. You'll thank yourself when the window grows. A plain Toplevel is non-modal: the user can click back and forth between it and the main window. That's perfect for a search box, a palette, or a second view of the same data. Because the window is non-modal, the user can leave it open and keep working. The buttons reach back into root because root is in scope. That's the whole trick: a Toplevel is just another container, so variables from the outer function work inside it. A modal window freezes the rest of the app until the user closes it — exactly what you want for a confirmation or a required form.

"I want a program that analyses text files" is not a plan — it's a wish. It doesn't say what numbers to show, how the user picks the file, what the screen looks like, or what happens with a 50 MB novel. Programming starts by refusing to stay vague. The three dots are honest, but they're also a warning: if you can't name the steps, you can't code them. So before any widgets appear, sit down and write out what success looks like. A feature list is just a set of sentences, one per thing the program must do. 1. The user picks a .txt file from disk. 2. The program reads the file's text. 3. It counts: total characters, characters excluding spaces, words, lines. 4. It counts how often each word appears and shows the top results. 5. The results appear in the window, not in the terminal. 6. If something goes wrong (file missing, unreadable), the user sees a message instead of a crash. Each sentence is small enough to map onto a function or a widget. If a sentence is still doing two jobs, split it. "Read the file and count everything" is really two steps; keep them separate and the code will be testable. A quick sketch decides your layout before you're emotionally attached to a bad one. No a

A Frame is a plain rectangular container you put widgets into so they move and resize as a group. It draws nothing by default, which is exactly what you want when all you need is structure. Two frames, one for the button row and one for the main display, sit inside root. Anything you later add to top frame stays in the top strip; anything in body frame owns the rest of the window. That separation is what stops a growing program from turning into spaghetti. Tkinter cannot decide between two layout managers for one container, so it raises tkinter.TclError: cannot use geometry manager grid inside . which already has slaves managed by pack. Pick one manager per container and stick with it. In this book the choice is easy: use pack for the big vertical regions, use grid inside each region for column-and-row layouts. grid puts widgets into rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. sticky decides how a widget expands inside its cell. sticky="w" (west) glues the widget to the left edge of its cell instead of letting it float centred. Labels lined up at "w" read cleanly in a column. padx and pady give you breathing room — without them every widget touches its neighbours. Cells resize to fit the

A logic function takes plain Python values and returns plain Python values. It never touches tk, never reads an Entry, never updates a Label. count stats returns a dict, top words returns a list of tuples. Both are printable, comparable, and completely unaware that a GUI exists. That's the boundary: anything past it can be tested with print() in a shell. A method on your App class is allowed to cross the boundary, because its job is translation: read from widgets, call logic, push results back. analyse is the bridge. Everything above it is GUI, everything below it is data. Notice that it calls count stats and immediately feeds the result into configure calls — that handoff is the only place the two worlds touch. Inline logic seems faster to write, but now the counting is welded to the button and can't be reused or tested. The moment you want the same numbers from a different source — a pasted string, a URL, a unit test — you have to copy the code. Keep it in a function and call that function. If your counting module imports tkinter, the boundary has collapsed. Logic functions should run in a bare Python shell. The only tk import belongs in the file that builds the interface. A clea

One callback does four jobs in order: ask for a path, guard against cancel, read the bytes, hand the text to the display method. askopenfilename returns "" on cancel, so if not path: return is the guard. The with block handles closing the file. Once the text is in memory, self. display(text) takes over — and because display only expects a string, you could hand it text from anywhere and the rest of the program wouldn't notice. If you read the file during init , there's no path yet and the program either errors or reads the wrong thing. File reading is an action the user triggers, so it belongs in a callback connected to a button or menu item — never in the constructor. The design so far analyses text but never lets the user see or edit it. A Text widget in its own frame fixes that. wrap="word" keeps words intact at line breaks instead of cutting them mid-word. Expand it with fill="both", expand=True so it grows with the window. Now display can also drop the loaded text into this widget before counting it. self.text widget only exists if the builder method assigned to it. Forgetting self. on the assignment means the attribute is never created, and every later reference raises Attrib

Every file read can fail for reasons outside your control. Wrap it, report it, and don't crash. OSError covers FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, and the rest of the filesystem failures in one catch. Showing str(e) gives the user a real reason ("Permission denied") instead of a blank error box. parent=self.root keeps the dialog attached to your window. except: with no exception type catches SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt, and your own NameError bugs, making the program impossible to quit or debug. Always name the exception you expect (OSError, ValueError). If you must catch broadly during development, write except Exception as e: and log it. UTF-8 is a good default but not a guarantee — a file from an older Windows program may be cp1252 or latin-1. Offer a fallback: latin-1 can decode any byte sequence without raising, so it's a safe last resort — the characters may look odd but the program keeps running. You could also ask the user which encoding to use, but that's usually more than a learning project needs. An empty editor isn't an error, but the results screen should say something sensible instead of showing four zeros and a blank list. text.strip() is empty for a file containin

A Canvas is, at its core, a rectangular blank area on which you can draw arbitrary shapes, place text, and drop in images. It is the only tkinter widget that says "draw whatever you like." The labels and buttons we used earlier are like预制 components — their appearance and behaviour are fixed in advance. A Canvas, on the other hand, is a blank sheet of paper. With it you can build progress bars, flowcharts, a simple drawing pad, or even a small game. Why do we need it? Sooner or later you will hit a requirement that standard widgets simply cannot express: a rounded button, a set of annotated points on a picture, a drag-and-drop connector tool. These all rely on the Canvas. Like every other widget, you create it first and lay it out afterwards: When you run this you will see a large white rectangle. At the moment it is empty — a canvas does not draw anything by itself; it only provides a place to draw. Parameter reference: Parameter Meaning --- --- width / height Canvas width and height in pixels bg Background colour, light grey by default highlightthickness Thickness of the focus border; set it to 0 to hide the dashed frame This is the single most important rule for the Canvas: the

The core shapes the Canvas can draw are just these; memorise them and you are set: Method What it draws Argument form --- --- --- create rectangle(x1,y1,x2,y2) Rectangle Top-left + bottom-right create oval(x1,y1,x2,y2) Oval Opposite corners of the bounding box create line(x1,y1,x2,y2,...) Straight line Multiple points joined in order create polygon(x1,y1,x2,y2,...) Polygon All vertices create arc(x1,y1,x2,y2) Arc Opposite corners of the bounding box Notice that ovals and arcs are both positioned using a bounding rectangle. You supply a rectangular frame and tkinter draws the largest oval that fits inside it. fill sets the interior colour and outline sets the border colour. The default is a black border; if you want no border at all, write outline="". create line accepts any number of points and joins them in sequence: Common options: Option Meaning --- --- fill Line colour width Line thickness in pixels dash Dash pattern, e.g. (5, 3) means 5 on, 3 off arrow Arrowhead: tk.FIRST / tk.LAST / tk.BOTH smooth Set to True to turn the polyline into a smooth curve create polygon is like create line, but it automatically joins the last point back to the first to form a closed shape: The argu

create text(x, y, text="...") writes text at the given coordinates. Important: this point is the text's "anchor point", which by default sits at the text's centre. Common options: Option Meaning --- --- text The text to display font A tuple (family, size, style); style may be "bold" or "italic" fill Text colour anchor Anchor position: tk.CENTER (default), tk.NW (top-left), etc. justify Multi-line alignment: tk.LEFT / tk.CENTER / tk.RIGHT By default anchor=tk.CENTER, so the coordinates (200, 50) mark the centre of the text. If you want the coordinates to mean the top-left corner, set anchor=tk.NW: The eight anchor constants are N, S, E, W, NE, NW, SE, SW and CENTER. Memory aid: N is up, S is down, E is right, W is left, and combinations give you the corners. On a Windows machine, font=("SimHei", 20) displays Chinese just fine, but on Linux or macOS you may get empty boxes (missing glyphs). When writing an interface for several platforms, do not assume a particular font is installed; either leave the font parameter at its default or use tkinter's font.Font object to discover what is available. For this lesson, the key point is simply: "state the font you need explicitly." To display

As we saw earlier, every shape you draw returns an integer ID. Every operation uses that ID: rect and oval are the IDs , and you use them to operate on those two shapes. canvas.move(id, dx, dy) moves the shape by dx pixels (horizontally) and dy pixels (vertically) relative to its current position: This is the basis of animation — move a little, refresh, move a little more, and the shape appears to move (covered in detail in Lesson 7). dx and dy may be negative: a negative dx goes left and a negative dy goes up. canvas.coords(id, x1, y1, x2, y2) moves the shape to a brand-new position in one step. The difference from move is that move means "take a few more steps", while coords means "teleport it over there". Keep the two uses clear: Method Semantics Typical use --- --- --- move(id, dx, dy) Relative movement Animation, dragging coords(id, x1, y1, x2, y2) Absolute positioning Precise placement, resetting a position If you call coords(id) without supplying new coordinates, it returns the current coordinate list [x1, y1, x2, y2]. This is a very handy trick for reading the shape's present position. canvas.itemconfig(id, options) lets you change a shape's colour, border and other propert

Goal: as the mouse is dragged across the canvas it leaves a trail, and a button clears the canvas. The key actions: pressing the mouse "puts the pen down", dragging it "draws a continuous line", and releasing it "lifts the pen". These correspond neatly to three mouse events. A Canvas plus a Button, laid out with pack: This gives you a white canvas with a button. At this point you cannot draw anything yet , because no mouse events have been bound. The Canvas has three crucial mouse events: Event When it fires What we use it for --- --- --- <ButtonPress-1> Left button pressed Record the "put pen down" point <B1-Motion> Left button held while moving Draw from the previous point to the current one <ButtonRelease-1> Left button released End this stroke In <B1-Motion>, B1 stands for Button 1 (the left button). While you hold and move, it fires at high frequency, and each time it fires we draw one short segment. The core idea: each time we drag, take the current coordinates, join them to the "previous point" with a short line, then update the current point so it becomes the new "previous point". A chain of tiny segments produces a stroke. The event object carries coordinates: event.x and

Requirement: make a square move 5 pixels every 50 milliseconds to simulate "automatic movement". The intuitive version: This version freezes the program completely. Why? Because tkinter's event loop (mainloop) is hijacked by your while loop and can never move on to redraw the window or handle the mouse. tkinter uses a single-threaded, event-driven model: mainloop() constantly "fetches an event, processes it, redraws the interface". Once you put while True inside a handler , the event loop is stuck in that infinite loop and cannot escape — it cannot fetch the next event, cannot redraw, and cannot respond to a window drag. It may even ignore a click on the close button (forcing you to terminate the program from the operating system). widget.after(milliseconds, function) means: "call this function after this many milliseconds." It does not block and wait; instead it "registers" a future task with the event loop, then returns immediately so mainloop can keep running. The key point: move step registers the next after call before it returns. That way the event loop is free after each move to handle other events and redraw the display. This is "recursive timing" — the function schedules i

Animation = move the shape a little at fixed time intervals and redraw it. The persistence of vision in the human eye joins those consecutive frames into "motion". A "frame" is one complete cycle of "move plus redraw". In tkinter, move already triggers a redraw implicitly, so as long as you keep moving, the picture animates. A ball is just a circle (an oval). Let us put one on the canvas: Define a global variable dx for "how many pixels the ball moves in the x direction per frame": Use coords() to read the current position and decide whether to bounce: The secret of a bounce is to negate the velocity: when the ball hits the right wall, dx = -dx sends it back to the left. Run it: a red ball bounces around the window, reversing direction whenever it hits an edge. You might wonder: why not track a "ball position variable" and test the boundary against that? Because after move, the ball's actual coordinates are managed inside the Canvas. Reading them with coords() is always accurate. Keep the data source single: the coordinates live in the Canvas, and we only read them when we need them. This approach also supports "many balls at once" naturally — each ball reads its own coordinates, w

Recall the bouncing ball from Lesson 7: move dx=4 pixels per frame, one frame every 20 milliseconds. That "200 pixels per second" is an ideal value calculated on paper. In reality: On a fast computer, after(20, ...) really does fire every 20 ms → speed is close to 200 On a busy computer (many programs running), the actual interval is 40 ms → speed is only 100 On a slower computer with an even lower frame rate → the animation is slower still The same code runs at different speeds in different environments. In a game this is fatal: Alice's ball reaches the goal in 2 seconds while Bob's takes 4. Delta time (abbreviated dt) is "how much time has passed since the previous frame". Its unit is seconds (or milliseconds). Scale the movement amount by dt and "movement speed" becomes "pixels per second", independent of the frame rate. A large dt (long frame interval) means a large movement; a small dt (short interval) means a small movement. The average speed stays constant. Python's standard library time.time() returns the current timestamp in seconds: Use it to calculate dt inside an animation: The key change: canvas.move(ball, speed dt, 0). When dt is 0.02 seconds (20 ms per frame), the mo

A keyboard event can be bound to "a specific widget" or to "the whole window (root)". The difference is that a binding on a widget only fires when that widget has focus (is selected), whereas a binding on root works globally. Bind one function to each arrow key and move with move: Run it: press the arrow keys and the square moves by the step size. Symptom: the binding is there, but pressing the arrow keys does not move the square. Cause: focus is on another widget or window. A Canvas binding only fires when the Canvas itself has focus. The game has three elements: a ball, a paddle and a score. In the same directory as main.py, named save.json — simplest, works across machines. JSON is a text format that looks almost identical to a Python dictionary. Saving trilogy: open + json.dump + close the file. Loading: json.load gives you a dictionary directly. ensure ascii=False is important — without it, Chinese becomes garbled escape sequences like \u5c0f\u660e. indent=2 adds line breaks and indentation, so you can open it in Notepad and read it. Pattern: read the save on startup (use defaults if no file exists), write the save on exit (or whenever the score updates). Most likely cause: forgot to handle the QUIT event, or the main loop never even started. A more insidious freeze: an infinite loop outside the main loop. Many beginners open their IDE the moment they get the assignment. Halfway through, they realise that "category" and "tag" are two different things and the database has to be rebuilt. Or they finish the interface, only to discover that what the user really wanted was "a monthly summary", not "a complete list of every transaction". The project in this book is called Ledger (a personal expense tracker). It is small enough to finish in a week or two, yet large enough to walk you through every part of a desktop application: how data is stored, how the interface is laid out, how charts are drawn, and finally how everything is packaged for someone else to run. Before you type a single line of code, write down the answers to these three questions: 1. Who is this for? (For the author to track personal spending — single user, single computer.) 2. What must it do? (Record an income or expense, view the history, group totals by category, and persist the data to disk.) 3. What will it not do? (No multi-user support, no cloud sync, no budget reminders.) The answers to these three questions decide every technical choice that follows. A transaction is a core database concept. It guarantees that a group of operations either all succeed or all fail; it never stops halfway. A ledger scenario: a user wants to change a £100 "Food" entry to "Transport" and add a note at the same time. Those two steps should be tied together — if the first succeeds and the second fails, the database is left inconsistent. A world without transactions: a network blip, a program crash or a full disk could leave a group of operations half done. With transactions, any problem lets you rollback() to the state before the operations began. By default, SQLite is "deferred commit": INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must be followed by an explicit commit. But autocommit can be switched on: each statement commits immediately with no manual commit. For a small desktop program that saves a few lines of code, but at the cost of losing atomicity — multiple statements can no longer be grouped. This project stays with manual commit because "add one record" looks simple now, but later you may want "insert a record + update a statistics cache + write a log" in the same transaction. Keeping transaction support makes that flexible. sqlite3.connect() returns a connection

A desktop program faces real users, not just you. You would never delete ledger.db by hand, type "two hundred quid" in the amount box, or try to write while the C drive has 1KB free. Your users will. A program with no exception handling crashes like this: The window vanishes, the user loses data, gets a fright, and never opens it again. This is not a UX issue, it is a trust issue. tkinter has a quirk: exceptions thrown inside callbacks are printed to the console by default and the program keeps running, but an uncaught exception that escapes the event loop brings the whole thing down. The fix is a global hook. Python's sys.excepthook is called whenever any uncaught exception occurs: Three rules: 1. Print the full stack first — that is the developer's debugging trail, the user never sees it. 2. Then show a friendly messagebox — tell the user what happened and what to do, no stack dump. 3. Put it at the very top of main.py , before any business code runs. tkinter's own exceptions travel a different path , and some GUI frameworks swallow exceptions in the event loop. As a belt-and-braces measure, still wrap your own callbacks in try/except. Scenario: the user keeps the ledger on a USB

Languages split roughly in two. Understanding the difference explains why "the environment" matters so much. Compiled (e.g. C) : you write the whole book, hire a translator to render it into English in one go, then hand the English version to the reader. Slow to translate, fast to read. Interpreted (e.g. Python) : you say a sentence, the translator renders it, the listener hears it. Python is the latter. It has a program called the interpreter , which reads your code and executes it line by line. Two direct consequences: 1. Upside : write one line, run it immediately — experimentation is nearly free. Perfect for learning. 2. Cost : you must have a correct interpreter installed, otherwise your code is just ordinary text. So "setting up an environment" boils down to one sentence: This site you're reading runs Python by itself. That's not uploading your code to some server — it uses Pyodide , which compiles real CPython (the official Python interpreter) into a format the browser can execute, running entirely on your own machine. Python abstracts "an ordered row of elements" into a concept called a sequence . Lists, tuples, and strings are concrete types of sequence. To tell whether something is a sequence, check whether it supports these operations: fetching by index, slicing, asking for its length, and testing membership. Every operation in the next section works on all three . All start at 0, and all support negative indexes (-1 is the last). The half-open rule is identical for all three. A string's in asks "does this substring occur", not "is this single character present". That differs subtly from checking for an element in a list, so do not conflate the two. The types must match: a list can only concatenate with a list, never with a tuple or a string. To concatenate different types, convert them to the same type first: repeats a sequence several times. Suppose you want to store a few people's scores in a list: Question: what is Alice's score? You cannot tell . A list remembers "which position", not "who is who". To find Alice you must keep a parallel list of names: It works, but the two lists must stay perfectly aligned — miss by one and everything is wrong. A dictionary binds the name and the score together: "Alice" is the key , and 92 is its value . Keys and values come in pairs, joined by a colon :. The whole dictionary sits inside curly braces { }. To find Alice's score you write scores["Alice"] — you never need to know she is "number three" . The most common way to build a dictionary is a literal — writing the key-value pairs directly: You can also start empty and add entries afterwards (covered in detail in Lesson 12): The dict() constructor builds a dictionary from key=value arguments. For a string key you must write the literal form {"Alice": 92}. A dictionary is a lookup table : give it a key, get the value ba

This is the single most common source of dictionary errors. For safer lookups you have two options. In a dictionary, in tests whether the key is present, not the value. The rule for get(key, default) is: if the key exists, return its value; if it does not, return the default you supplied . With no default, get returns None: ⚠️ Crash: treating get's default as something that "writes into the dictionary". get is read-only : it never writes a "Carol": 0 entry. It just hands you a fallback value when it cannot find the key; the dictionary itself is untouched. Adding an entry and changing an entry look exactly the same — both are square-bracket assignment: The only test is whether the key exists. Present means update; absent means create. ⚠️ Crash: thinking "add" and "update" are two different operations. You do not need two rules. The short version: a dictionary key must be an immutable object. Strings, numbers, and tuples are fine as keys; lists and dictionaries are not. The keyword in the error is unhashable . It really means: "this thing can change, so I cannot use it as an index." A dictionary fetches values quickly because of a hash table : Python computes a "hash value" for each key to decide where that entry lives. If a key could change, its hash would change — computed once when stored and once when looked up, the two would differ, and the value could never be found. So Python simply refuses mutable objects as keys — the problem is prevented at the language level. ⚠️ Crash: assuming "a tuple is always usable as a key". A tuple is immutable, but if it contains a mutable object it still cannot be a key: The first element of the tuple is a list. The real test is that the key object and everything inside it must be immutable . Scenario: a pile of votes, words, or cities — and you want to know how many times each one occurs . Use a dictionary as a counter : the key is the item, the value is the count. The logic is clear: seen before means add one; never seen means record one. ⚠️ Crash: incrementing a key you have not seen yet. A set is written with braces, and the elements are separated by commas: It looks a lot like a dictionary because both use { }, but a set has no colon and no key-value pairs . ⚠️ Crash: using {} to build an empty set. {} means an empty dictionary . To build an empty set you must use set(): Remember: {} is a dict; set() is the empty set . This is one of Python's most counter-intuitive corners. set(sequence) drops the duplicates for you. This is the single most classic use of a set — deduplication . Inside a set the same element can appear only once . Add it ten times and the set still keeps one copy: add(element) adds one element. If it already exists, Python ignores the request silently — no error. ⚠️ Crash: assuming add allows duplicates the way a list's append does. A set is naturally self-deduping. So if you need "a bunch of things that may repeat", use a list; if you need "one copy of each", use a set. A set's killer feature is that in is extremely fast — whether the set holds one hundred or one million elements, asking "is it in there?" takes essentially the same amount of time. Why it is fast is the main topic of Lesson 18. For now, just remember how to use it and how it feels

To intersect lists you must convert first — use a set, or a list comprehension. The union is all the elements from both sets, with overlaps counted only once . The symbol is (the vertical bar). Notice that "Bob" appears only once — the union dedupes automatically. A real scenario: merging user lists from two sources. ⚠️ Crash: using + to combine two sets. Let us run a little thought experiment and just count how many comparisons have to happen . Imagine you are looking for someone in a list. The list holds ten thousand names, and the person you want — "Alice" — happens to be last. A list is a single line: to find something you must walk from the front to the back . The first one is not a match, neither is the second... you keep going until the 9,999th entry before you finally find it. If you are unlucky and "Alice" is at the very end or does not exist at all, you have to compare against all ten thousand names before giving up. A set does not check things one by one. Instead it first turns each name into a number , then uses that number to jump straight to the right slot and look there — a hit means it is found. ⚠️ The key difference: a list compares; a set calculates. Looking in a list: compare one by one , up to ten thousand comparisons Looking in a set: calculate a number once and jump straight to the slot — one check That is why, whether a set holds a thousand or a million elements, membership tests take essentially the same amount of time , while a list gets slower the more items it holds. Imagine you are writing a small class-score tool and need to grade each student: Three nearly identical blocks. Now suppose the requirement changes — you need four bands, "excellent / good / pass / fail". You would have to edit three places , and by the time you reach the third your hand slips and a bug appears. That is the true cost of copying and pasting: logic should live in exactly one place; writing it three times plants three landmines . The idea behind a function is almost embarrassingly simple: wrap the logic, give it a name, then call the name whenever you need it . Three duplicated blocks have become one . def means "define", judge is the name of this logic, and score is "what you feed into it". Say judge(92) and Python runs that logic. ⚠️ Crash: trying to call a function before defining it. Python executes top to bottom. greet("Alice") appears before the definition, so the interpreter has never heard of greet and raises NameError. Define first, then call — the order cannot be reversed. A function has four parts: the def keyword, a name, parameters in parentheses, and an indented block after the colon. def tells Python: I'm about to define a function add is the name — it should say what the function does (a, b) are the parameters; you supply the two numbers when you call it after the colon : you must indent (usually 4 spaces); the indented lines are the function body Calling it: ⚠️ Crash: forgetting to indent after the colon. Python uses indentation to decide which lines belong to the function. Forget it and the interpreter complains immediately. return also has to sit inside the indented block, otherwise it isn't part of the function at all. Parameters are how a function receives information from the outside. Separate several with commas: The values you pass in when calling are called arguments (the actual values: 3, "Ada"), while a and first in the definition are parameters (the formal names). ⚠️ Crash: the wrong number of arguments. Too few or too many, either way you get a TypeError. The most common style: arguments are lined up against parameters by position. The first argument "Beijing" goes to city, the second "Alice" goes to name — they are matched by position . ⚠️ Crash: swapping the arguments produces the wrong meaning, with no error. This does not raise anything, but the meaning is completely backwards. When the parameters are all the same type (here, both are strings), swapping them is very hard to spot. Good parameter names help reviewers catch this just by reading the call. When one parameter almost always takes the same value, give it a default: scheme="https" is a default argument. If you skip it, the default is used; if you pass one, yours wins. ⚠️ Crash: putting a default argument before a positional one. Python's rule is: defaults must come after positionals . The reason is "match the positional ones first, then fill the rest with defaults"; reverse the order and the interpreter cannot decide which position goes where. The iron rule: positionals first, defaults after . When you call a function you can say which parameter each value belongs to: Writing name= lets you ignore the order, and it reads more clearly. ⚠️ Crash: a positional argument afte

The basic case: compute a result, hand it back with return. The caller gets whatever stands after return — it can be stored in a variable, put in a list, or passed straight into another function. Python lets you return several values, separated by commas: It looks like "two values came back", but only one thing was returned: a tuple with two elements . The line first, last = ... is tuple unpacking (Lesson 6): the two elements of the tuple are assigned to two variables. The function never "returned two things"; it returned one tuple. ⚠️ Crash: thinking you got several values, then indexing them wrong. This is not wrong, but it feeds the illusion of "several things came back". Remember: return a, b is exactly the same as return (a, b). ⚠️ Crash: the number of variables does not match. stats returns a 3-tuple, but you only gave it two names. The tuple size and the variable count must agree (unless you use to collect the rest — covered later). Once return runs, the function ends on the spot; nothing after it executes. That makes it great for "bailing out": This style — handle the bad cases first, then do the real work — is called a guard clause , and it is far cleaner than nested if/el

A variable defined inside a function exists only inside that function — the outside cannot see it: result is local to calc , and it "disappears" when the function ends. The outside world never knew it existed. ⚠️ Crash: expecting a name defined inside a function to survive outside. This is one of the most common beginner assumptions. A function's job is to isolate : its insides are hidden; by default, its outsides are visible (see below). A function can read a variable from outside: But it cannot casually change it: Why? Because Python sees counter += 1 assigning to counter and decides counter is a local variable . That line first reads counter and then adds 1, but the local counter has not been assigned yet — hence UnboundLocalError. ⚠️ Crash: reading is fine, assigning blows up. The very same name counter: read it and it is treated as outside; assign to it and it becomes local. Python decides based on "is there an assignment to it inside the function?", not on what you intended. To change a global variable from inside a function, declare it with global: global counter means: "do not make a new local variable; I want the global one." ⚠️ Crash: forgetting global, and changing nothi

In Python, a function is an object just like a number, a string or a list — it lives in memory, and def simply binds a name to it. greet is a variable name pointing at a function object in memory. type and id both work on it — that is proof positive of "object". ⚠️ Crash: forgetting the parentheses and getting the function itself. get greeting is the function object; get greeting() is the call. Miss the parentheses and you get "the function", not "its return value". Since a function is an object, you can give it another name — and that name is callable too: calc = square has no parentheses , meaning "hand me that function, I want a name for it too" — not "call it". ⚠️ Crash: accidentally adding parentheses at assignment, which calls it on the spot. square(5) calls the function and returns 25, so calc becomes the integer 25 — calling it again blows up. No parentheses = the function itself; with parentheses = its return value. Functions can live in lists and dictionaries, so you can manage a whole family of behaviours in one container : ops is a "function list"; iterating it runs each operation in turn. This is wonderfully handy for calculators and menu-driven programs. ⚠️ Crash: cal

Factorial n! = n × (n-1) × ... × 1 is defined in terms of a smaller version of itself: The execution unfolds like this: Each step makes the problem a little smaller, until it reaches the smallest case (n<=1) and stops. ⚠️ Crash: forgetting the stopping condition. Each recursive call must make the problem smaller , moving towards the stopping condition. n decreases by 1 each time and eventually reaches 0, hitting the stopping condition. If you wrote count down(n) without subtracting 1, it would never reach 0 and would always blow up. The Fibonacci sequence: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8... (each number is the sum of the previous two). A file's lifetime is "until you delete it". So to make data survive a restart, you must move it from memory to disk — that's file I/O . Don't overthink it. After a PySide6 program starts, only one "main thread" is doing the work. That thread has two jobs: running your business logic, and running the event loop. The event loop constantly handles mouse clicks, keyboard input, and repaint requests to keep the interface "alive". Key fact: app.exec() is that while loop. Your on clicked() slot is called from inside the event loop. Until on clicked() returns, the event loop is stuck there — new clicks cannot get in, repaint requests cannot be processed, and the window goes "not responding". After clicking that button, the window freezes completely — you cannot drag it, you cannot click it, and the system may flag it as "not responding". This is not a bug; the event loop is being strangled by your time.sleep(5). One-line rule: any operation taking more than 100ms has no business in a main-thread slot. The human perception threshold is roughly 100ms — past that, the interface feels noticeably "laggy". QThread is Qt's thread wrapper. The core pattern: create a QThread object + a Worker object, use moveToThread to move the Worker onto the background thread, and trigger the Worker's work via signals. Flow: thread.start() → fires the started signal → calls worker.do work() → do work runs on the background thread → reports progress back to the main thread via the progress signal → when done → quit() ends the thread. Three steps: ① create QThread ② moveToThread ③ connect the startup logic with a signal. Key point: the Worker must have no parent object. If you pass a parent when constructing the Worker, moveToThread will fail — Qt does not allow a QObject with a parent to cross threads. The Worker's signals are the bridge between the main thread and the background thread. The background thread must not touch the UI directly; it emits signals, which connect to slots on the main thread, and Qt schedules the cross-thread call automatically. Symptom: the program runs for a while, then crashes with Cannot send events to objects owned by a different thread — or a raw segmentation fault. A proxy model is itself a model. The view has no idea it is talking to a proxy; it treats it like any ordinary model, and the proxy in turn asks the real source model for data. By default, sorting is done on the DisplayRole — which is text. To sort numerically, you must tell the proxy which role to use. Header-click sorting is literally one line: setSortingEnabled(True). Qt's widget library covers about 90% of everyday needs. Buttons, input fields, tables, menus, sliders, progress bars, tabs... if you can snap pieces together, that is the cheapest and most correct answer. QSS can change colour, rounded corners, borders, gradients, and states — covered in the previous volume, "Qt Advanced 1", and not repeated here. QSS solves "style", never "behaviour". QSS can change "the look of parts that already exist": background, border, radius, font, padding. A Promise is a container for a result that will only be available at some future moment . It separates "the asynchronous operation" from "what to do once you have the result." new Promise accepts an executor function , which is executed synchronously right away. The parameters resolve and reject are provided by the JS engine. Subsequent calls to resolve/reject are ignored. Debounce: after a trigger, wait a while — and if another trigger arrives in that window, reset the timer . The function only actually runs after things have been quiet for long enough. The classic use case is search-as-you-type . A user types "L", "Lo", "Lon", "London" — you don't want a request per keystroke, just one request after they stop typing . Throttle: no matter how often it's triggered, run at most once in every time window . The classic use case is infinite scroll . The user scrolls frantically — you don't want dozens of callbacks per second, just at most one every 200ms . Why it crashes: If debounce(doSearch, 300) runs over and over, it creates a new function with a fresh timer every time , so the calls can never share a timer — and the debounce silently stops working. Why it crashes: A canvas has two "size" concepts — the drawing buffer size (the HTML width/height) and the display size (the CSS width/height). You have probably ordered food on your phone. That app is a program full of rules: if the user taps this button, then show that screen. Parameter: the name inside the parentheses when you define the function. It acts like a placeholder variable. Argument: the actual value you pass in when you call the function. When the function runs, the argument's value is copied into the parameter, and the function body can then use that name. Separate parameters with commas in the definition, and separate arguments with commas in the call: Positional matching: the first argument goes to the first parameter, the second to the second. Order matters. When an argument is missing, the parameter's value is undefined. We first met this back in lesson 2 — any variable without a value is undefined. So before using a parameter, it is wise to check: A shorter way is a default value , written with = right after the parameter: name = "guest" means: if nobody passes name, automatically use "guest". Consequence: 3 + undefined gives NaN. Mismatched argument counts do not throw an error, but produce bizarre results — one of the hardest bugs to track down. return expression means: take the value of that expression and hand it back to whoever called the function. The caller can store it in a variable, print it, or feed it into another calculation. Compare a function with return against one without: console.log only displays something on the screen; return actually hands data back. This is the single most common confusion for slow-track learners. Every function that runs to the end without hitting a return gives back undefined. This is the same logic as "a variable with no value is undefined" from lesson 2. The moment return executes, the function stops dead — everything after it is skipped: This is the early return technique: when a condition is met, return immediately instead of nesting layers of if-else. Consequence: the value is undefined. Always put the value you want to return right after return, otherwise it is the same as return undefined. Consequence: for scores below 60 the function reaches the end with no return, producing undefined. To manipulate a web page, JS uses a global object called document — it is the root of the tree: Remember this sentence: document is the bridge between JS and the web page. Only after step 3 does the element actually appear in the page. div is the parent of h1 and p. h1 and p are the children of div. h1 and p are siblings of each other. addEventListener("click", function) means: when the user clicks this button, run this function. Approach one: onclick (not recommended) Approach two: addEventListener (recommended) onclick is a property assignment, and the second assignment overwrites the first; addEventListener can attach any number of handlers. Real projects almost always use addEventListener. To trigger a form submission from code, use form.dispatchEvent(new Event("submit")). A better technique is "event delegation": attach one listener to the parent and use e.target to figure out which child was clicked.
